builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
summary: Replaces trust in repository rules files (e.g., AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) as a security or compliance control with deterministic gates in front of sensitive endpoints, plus hidden-test-based evaluation. Cost is low in compute but requires building gate infrastructure around tool calls and accepting that a rules file may reduce agent task performance (Codex CLI: 99.0 to 67.7 percent). Failure modes: the study could not test the file's effect at HTTP boundaries due to a run-script error, results cover four agents and small repositories, and planted-package/instruction risks remain if no gate exists (7 of 45 ungated runs crossed).
rationale: Any team deploying coding agents in production should replace reliance on rules files with enforced gates, since the study shows rules files are advisory at best and can measurably degrade agent correctness.
technique: Enforced gates over rules files for coding agents

claims.statement: Replaces trust in repository rules files (e.g., AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) as a security or compliance control with deterministic gates in front of sensitive endpoints, plus hidden-test-based evaluation. Cost is low in compute but requires building gate infrastructure around tool calls and accepting that a rules file may reduce agent task performance (Codex CLI: 99.0 to 67.7 percent). Failure modes: the study could not test the file's effect at HTTP boundaries due to a run-script error, results cover four agents and small repositories, and planted-package/instruction risks remain if no gate exists (7 of 45 ungated runs crossed).

Across four coding agents, a rules file rarely prevented boundary-crossing attempts, and for Codex CLI it cut hidden-test pass rate from 99.0% to 67.7%; pooled passes fell 7.7 points, while only a hard gate reliably blocked forbidden requests.
